newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Peres won't help Netanyahu beat back hawks. [CORRECTED 12:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Peres won't help Netanyahu beat back hawks. [CORRECTED 12:30 GMT]

text.p: Israeli opposition leader Shimon Peres said on Sunday his Labour party would not enter a unity government to protect Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from a right-wing rebellion over peace moves.
"It is not on the agenda," Peres told Israeli Army radio.

At least eight Israeli hawks, irate over Netanyahu's decision to hand over more occupied West Bank lands to Palestinian rule, have threatened to bolt the ruling coalition that commands 66 seats in the 120-member parliament.
Under a decision narrowly endorsed by the cabinet on Friday over the objections of hardline ministers, Israel will hand over another nine percent of the occupied West Bank to full PLO rule.

Palestinians, already enraged over Netanyahu's plan to build Jewish homes in mainly Arab East Jerusalem, said he was giving too little. Israeli right-wingers said Netanyahu was giving too much of the biblical Land of Israel under U.S. and PLO pressure.
"We need to see how we can stand as one front against these pressures because this process does not lead to peace," said rebel legislator Zvi Hendel of the National Religious Party.
Israel has already handed over three percent of the West Bank and most of the Gaza Strip, territories it occupied in 1967, under an interim peace deal with the Palestinian Liberation Organisation.
Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said he expected detailed withdrawal plans for the pending redeployment from mainly rural areas of the West Bank to be submitted for his approval on Monday.
He told Israel Radio the pullback "would begin immediately afterwards". Under a peace deal with the PLO, Israel is to carry out three West Bank redeployments by mid-1998.
Netanyahu warned rebellious lawmakers he could circumvent them by inviting the centre-left Labour to join his Likud party in a unity government.

But Peres, who lost last May's election to Netanyahu, said joining forces with the Likud leader was unthinkable while the government remained the target of a police corruption probe over a failed appointment of an attorney-general.
"Until this issue ends, there is absolutely nothing to talk about," Peres said.

More that 20 top officials, including Netanyahu, have been questioned by police in the "Bar-On affair" -- a probe into allegations the short-lived appointment of attorney general Roni Bar-On in January was part of a criminal deal to help a key coalition member win a plea bargain in a corruption trial.
"(Coalition) members are ashamed to be part of this government," Ehud Barak, Peres' heir apparent, told the radio.
"We need to have a no-confidence vote on the first posssible day on Netanyahu's general management of the state of Israel," Barak said.

Netanyahu began meeting rightist critics on Sunday to try to keep his coalition together ahead of the Labour-initiated no-confidence vote slated for next week. A no-confidence vote requires the support of 61 legislators to topple the government.
Peres stressed that Netanyahu could still count on Labour's backing in any parliamentary confidence votes in support of peace moves.

Admitting government gridlock, Foreign Minister David Levy said Israel's interests were not served by inter-coalition battles over implementation of peace deals the government inherited from the Labour administration.

"There is continued difficulty that every step needs to be tested not between the coalition and the opposition...but within the coalition itself. This is unnatural and cannot answer the essential needs of state," Levy told Army radio.
